---
title: "Components of a generalized linear model"
---

A [**generalized linear model**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214), or [**GLM**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214), combines a response distribution from the exponential family, a linear predictor, and a link function. The [preceding page](link-functions.qmd) introduced the link and inverse link. The [next page on the exponential family](exponential-family.qmd) states the formal restriction on the response distribution. For now, normal, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions supply the examples.

Build the model in three steps. The
response family states what one response can be and how its variance relates to its mean, the linear predictor states how
predictors combine, and the inverse link maps that combination to a valid
conditional mean.

## Step 1: choose the response family

The response family must match the possible values of $Y$.

| response | possible family |
|---|---|
| continuous real-valued measurement | normal |
| binary choice | Bernoulli |
| nonnegative count | Poisson |

The family also specifies how the conditional variance relates to the conditional mean.

For a Bernoulli response, the mean is a probability $\pi_i$ and the variance is
$\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$. For a Poisson response, the mean and variance are both
$\lambda_i$. The family thus contributes more than the range of possible
observations.

## Step 2: recall the linear predictor

As introduced on the [design-matrix page](design-matrices.qmd), the [**linear predictor**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) is

$$
\eta_i
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}.
$$

Because the coefficients and predictor values are real numbers, $\eta_i$ can take any value on the real line.

The coefficients are additive on this scale. Increasing $x_{i1}$ by one changes $\eta_i$ by $\beta_1$ while other predictors are held fixed.

The linear predictor does not itself need to satisfy the response constraints.
It is an intermediate representation. A value of $\eta_i=3$ is neither a
probability nor an expected count until an inverse link interprets it.

## Step 3: use the inverse link

Let

$$
\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i].
$$

The [inverse-link function](link-functions.qmd) maps the unconstrained linear predictor into the mean values allowed by the response family:

$$
\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).
$$

Equivalently,

$$
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.
$$

For ordinary linear regression, the identity inverse link gives

$$
g^{-1}(\eta)=\eta.
$$

The conditional mean can be any real value, so no transformation is needed.

For a Bernoulli response, the inverse link must map the real line into $(0,1)$. For a count response, it must map into positive expected counts.

## Assemble a Bernoulli GLM

Suppose $Y_i=1$ marks an *in* completion and $Y_i=0$ marks a *for* completion.
Let $x_i$ be a centered duration measure. A Bernoulli GLM with an inverse-logit
mapping is

$$
Y_i\mid x_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,
$$

and

$$
\pi_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}.
$$

Take $\beta_0=-.40$ and $\beta_1=.70$. At $x=0$,

$$
\eta(0)=-.40
$$

and

$$
\pi(0)=\frac{1}{1+e^{.40}}\approx.401.
$$

At $x=2$,

$$
\eta(2)=-.40+.70(2)=1.00
$$

and

$$
\pi(2)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-1}}\approx.731.
$$

The duration contrast changes the linear predictor by $1.4$ and the completion
probability by about $.330$ over this particular interval.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-bernoulli-glm-means
#| echo: true
x <- c(0, 2)
eta <- -.40 + .70 * x
pi <- plogis(eta)

data.frame(x = x, eta = eta, probability = pi)
```

Each row now has a complete response distribution. At $x=0$, the model assigns
probability about $.401$ to response 1 and $.599$ to response 0. It does not
assign probability to values between them.

## Keep the two scales visible

A coefficient describes an additive change on the $\eta$ scale. The corresponding response-scale change depends on the inverse link.

With a nonlinear inverse link, the same coefficient-sized change in $\eta$ can produce different probability changes at different starting values.

Thus every GLM interpretation should state whether it concerns

1. the linear-predictor scale; or
2. the response-mean scale.

The distinction is particularly important for a nonlinear inverse link. The
coefficient $\beta_1=.70$ is a constant change in $\eta$ per duration unit. It
does not say that probability increases by $.70$, and it does not imply one
constant probability difference at every starting value.

## Do not omit the response distribution

Writing only

$$
\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)
$$

describes the conditional mean but leaves the observation statement implicit.
The full GLM also says that $Y_i$ is Bernoulli given that mean. This statement
supplies the conditional variance and the likelihood used for inference.

A mean equation is not a complete probability model. Omitting the response distribution makes it difficult to see whether the
family matches the measurement or which variation assumptions the fit uses.

## Check each part separately

These three model components suggest three checks:

1. Does the family assign probability only to possible observations?
2. Does the linear predictor contain the comparisons required by the theory?
3. Does the inverse link turn every possible $\eta$ into a valid mean?

A model can pass one check and fail another. A Poisson family has count support,
but a linear predictor may omit exposure. A valid inverse logit keeps
probabilities bounded, but the predictor may encode an uninterpretable category
contrast.

The next pages examine a common mathematical form for response families and the
data summaries those families retain.
